newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM says no way to slow inflation quickly.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM says no way to slow inflation quickly.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Tuesday that there was no way to slow Czech inflation quickly, and that central bank steps last year to slow consumer prices were more than the government wanted.
However, Klaus told the Zofin Forum of business leaders that February's inflation rate of 7.3 percent, year-on-year, was "satisfactory".

"At this moment I see in the Czech economy the existence of an array of short-term irremovable inflation factors which we cannot simply get rid of, and I also do not see any easy way to a faster slowing of inflation," said Klaus, a monetarist professor of economics.
Klaus took issue with restrictive monetary measures of the Czech National Bank last year which led to the lowering of inflation from levels above nine percent in the previous year.

"Basic structural characteristics of our economy decide how, in reality, the economic slowing is divided between a desired lowering of the inflation rate and undersirable lowering in the growth of output...and I am not sure that we (the government and the central bank) have the same opinion," Klaus said.
"I believe that in our context and in our structural parameters disinflation bought at the high price of a marked loss in the pace of economic growth was more than we would have wished," he added.
He said this discrepancy was a "serious affair" and something that economists in the upcoming period must "intensively" tackle.

Klaus said earlier that 1996 full-year gross domestic product growth ended one percent lower than the governement originally expected. He did not give a specific result, but the government's original forecast was for growth of 4.8 percent.
Full-year official GDP results are expected later this month.

Klaus said factors in this slowing of growth was weak demand for exports because of weak growth in protected markets in western Europe. Another reason was the "unfavourable structure of our domestic demand -- consumer as well as investment."

Klaus however stressed the "restrictive measures of the central bank" and its role on demand as a factor and said the CNB "used" the chaos after inconclusive June elections to raise interest rates and tighten minimum reserve requirements.
